org: S-Lab, Nanyang Technological University; University of Oxford; ACE Robotics
models: Astra (lead xhigh, members medium; paper does not give the full model name)
interface: One robot run as a team of persistent coding agents: each member owns a control group (arm+gripper, torso+chassis) and runs its own observe–reason–code–execute loop issuing end-effector/joint targets; a lead 'hyper-agent' assigns work, sets event-based waits, and can take over groups for coupled actions under exclusive control ownership
judged_by: human annotators with task-specific rubrics (physical progress, completion); operators monitor safety
trials: task-coverage: 72 rollouts over 25 task/platform settings; repeated-trial: 90 rollouts (6 tasks x 5 trials x 3 policies)

speed.latency: task-balanced mean 13.67 min (ACAP) vs 19.04 min (Direct) per task over 25 settings

summary: Splits a robot across asynchronous coding agents per control group, coordinated by a lead hyper-agent, on Galaxea R1 Pro and AgileX PiPER robots. 'Across 72 real-world rollouts covering 25 task/platform settings, ACAP reduces task-balanced time cost by 28.2% compared with a single-agent Direct Policy'; on repeated trials it lowers mean 30-min-capped cost on all six tasks (−29.4%), and on Collaborative tasks 'ACAP completes ten of ten runs, compared with eight for Direct and three for Fixed.'
caveats: Authors: 'The current framework does not include a dedicated motion-level collision-checking layer.' Evaluation is about time cost vs. the authors' own single-agent and fixed-delegation baselines; no learned-policy (VLA) comparison. Progress is human-annotated; operators monitor safety. The model is named only as 'Astra'. Releases a real-world rollout dataset.

name: NavRSI
title: NavRSI: Recursive Harness Self-Improvement for Vision-and-Language Navigation
org: Singapore Management University · Renmin University of China · Fudan University · Nanjing University of Science and Technology
interface: Frozen navigator LLM calls two tools, observe (single forward RGB view) and step (list of primitive actions: forward 0.25 m, turn 15°, STOP); a separate designer LLM (GPT-6-Astra in Codex CLI) rewrites the harness code over 8 RSI rounds using simulator diagnostics the navigator never sees
judged_by: VLN-CE standard metrics in simulator (NE/OSR/SR/SPL); real-world judging not stated
trials: R2R-CE-100: 3 runs per LLM; full R2R-CE and RxR-CE val-unseen splits; NavRAG-CE 100 episodes × 3 runs; real: 25 instructions × 4 runs on Unitree G1

speed.latency: RxR-CE mean 312.8 s per episode (vs 333.2 s NavGPT-3, 434.8 s MIP/Codex CLI)
speed.cost: $0.424 per RxR-CE episode with GPT-6-Astra (vs $0.562 NavGPT-3, $1.086 MIP)

summary: Vision-and-language navigation, not manipulation: a frozen frontier LLM steps a robot with primitive actions from one RGB camera, and a designer LLM recursively rewrites the harness. With GPT-6-Astra it reaches 85.64 SR on the full R2R-CE val-unseen split, '+4.13 SR over NavGPT-3, which pairs the same LLM with an 8B model'; the same harness beats native harnesses of four vendors by up to 11.3 SR. On a Unitree G1 humanoid: '48 SR against 36 for NavGPT-3 and 16 for Open-Nav'.
caveats: No limitations section. Navigation only; authors list extending 'to more embodied tasks beyond navigation' as future work. The full R2R-CE split includes the development set used for harness selection (held-out 537-episode comparison reported separately). Real-world run is 25 instructions × 4 runs with no stated judge. Source code 'will be released'.

name: Embodied-Harness
title: Embodied-Harness: Towards Recursive Self-Improvement for Robotic Manipulation
org: Zhejiang University · Huazhong University of Science and Technology
interface: Actor emits one of five control commands (move, rotate, point, gripper, home) with grounded arguments per step; harness converts to an SE(3) target pose and solves IK; a Reflector (same frozen model family) diagnoses each attempt and updates the harness guidance and hierarchical memory
judged_by: benchmark success checks (RoboTwin 2.0, RoboSPA, RMBench); real-world judging not stated
trials: 10 episodes per task on RoboTwin 2.0 (50 tasks), RoboSPA and real tasks (3 tasks, Piper arm); 20 per task on RMBench (9 tasks); max 45 interaction rounds per episode
summary: Actor/Reflector dual-agent harness around a frozen GPT-6 Astra that refines its harness from execution evidence. RoboTwin 2.0 C2R: 82.4% with zero demos, 'surpasses RoboDawn by 29.2 percentage points' and beats GigaBrain-0.7 (67.9%) and PrismWAM (75.5%); RoboSPA-Spatial L5 94.0%, RoboSPA-Long 59.5%, RMBench 94.4%. Real Piper arm: 'average success rate of 96.7% versus 40.0%' for π0.5.
caveats: No limitations section; authors' future work: 'experience transfer across tasks and embodiments and more efficient execution and reflection.' Headline numbers are after 4 harness-refinement rounds ('From round 0 to round 4, success rates increase from 59.2% to 82.4% on RoboTwin 2.0 C2R'), and the paper does not state a separate train/test split for refinement, so the 'zero-shot' comparison with RoboDawn is not like-for-like. Baseline numbers appear to be taken from prior reports. No latency, cost or code reported; real-world judge not stated.

name: EvoTER
title: EvoTER: Evolving Embodied Agents via Tool-Use Experience and Reflection
org: Institute of Automation, Chinese Academy of Sciences
interface: Codex-based agent selects one tool call per step (segmentation, detection, grasp generation, cuRobo motion planning, low-level control, a frozen VLA: Xiaomi-Robotics-1 in sim, a π0.5-based policy and Tether on the real robot) guided by a skill library; Explorer/Diagnoser/Validator roles (same frozen model) evolve the library, accepting revisions only on higher validation success
judged_by: 'externally evaluated task outcome' (RoboCasa365 checker in sim); real-world judge not stated
trials: Sim: RoboCasa365 Target50 (50 tasks), 3 evolution rounds × 5 exploration seeds and 5 validation seeds per task, frozen test set disjoint; real Franka: 5 test trials per task (3 short-horizon, 3 long-horizon tasks)

speed.cost: real-world development capped at 150 M total tokens per task; e.g. plate transfer 103.45 M → 17.58 M total tokens with sim initialization

summary: A frozen gpt-6.1-sol agent orchestrates a frozen VLA and analytic tools, and evolves a tool-use skill library that is kept only when complete-task validation success rises. RoboCasa365 Target50: 'from a pre-evolution baseline of 53.60% to 80.40%', vs Xiaomi-Robotics-1 57.40% and Harness VLA 59.20%. Real Franka long-horizon: 4/5, 5/5, 5/5 after real-world evolution vs 1/5 each by direct transfer.
caveats: Authors: 'Future work will streamline validation, reduce reliance on privileged simulation feedback, and broaden evaluation across tasks and embodiments.' Diagnoser can use privileged simulator state after stagnation (execution and validation use only ordinary tools). External baselines are 'taken from the cited sources'; Composite-Unseen 'development episodes ... may contribute to skill evolution'. Two-cup hanging needed 'a high-level hint' from humans. Real-world tests are 5 trials per task.

name: Real2Worlds2Real
title: Real2Worlds2Real: Scaling Self-Improving Agentic Real2Sim2Real for Robot Manipulation
interface: General-purpose coding agent with a skill-guided tool-orchestration harness writes Blender scripts and physics calibration to build digital twins/cousins, then writes code-as-policy programs (grasp + cuRobo/MPC), RL rewards, or trains ACT / Diffusion Policy with DAgger and RL decorators; distilled 'personal skills' are reused across tasks
judged_by: real: not stated; LIBERO-Pro: benchmark checker on 50 held-out initial states
trials: real: 30 trials per task per method (Dexmate robot with Sharpa hands); LIBERO-Pro Long: 20 tasks × 50 held-out initial states

speed.cost: world building for held-out lemon-cutting task: 28.1M → 13.9M tokens with skill reuse

summary: A GPT-6 Astra-powered agent turns real videos into digital twins and cousins, then develops policies in them for real deployment. Real dexterous robot (30 trials/task): 100.0% / 90.0% / 73.3% / 100.0% on Lift/PickPlace/Nut/Cup vs ASPIRE 90.0/86.7/63.3/80.0. On LIBERO-Pro Long with agent-written control scripts, 'as the library grows from 0 to 136 skills ... overall success rises from 52.9% to 82.2%'.
caveats: No limitations section. Real-robot policies are learned ACT/RL-decorator policies the agent trains, initialized from 60 real demonstrations; the frontier model is not in the runtime loop. LIBERO-Pro 82.2% appears to select the best candidate program ('Even the mean over all candidate programs, without selecting the best, rises from 44.1% to 69.1%'). Real-world judge not stated; no latency or dollar cost reported.

name: RoboColiseum
title: RoboColiseum: Co-evolution of Simulation, Evaluation, and Models
interface: Agent track: models run through the Agent2Act harness and 'directly generate robot-control commands' from observations and execution feedback; VLA track: π0.5, LingBot-VLA-2.0, GR00T N1.7 fine-tuned with 200 demos/task
judged_by: RoboColiseum test server (official fixed hidden set; budget-aware progress + completion score), plus human review for privileged-information exploits
trials: VLA: 50 robot–task configurations, 255 valid episodes per policy; Agent per-case denominators and inference-call counts not reported
summary: Sim platform with Real2Sim calibration (Pearson 0.9686 over 22 paired real–sim configurations) and an 8-track benchmark. Season II reports eight frontier-LLM Agent systems and three VLAs on the same four tracks (precision, cross-embodiment, whole-body, dexterous) but on separate leaderboards: Claude Fable 5.2 leads Agents with Overall 18.30 (precision 33.04); π0.5 leads VLAs with Overall 11.22. Agent dexterous scores 'remain low, spanning 0.00–5.19'.
caveats: Authors: 'differences in training, task coverage, and resource accounting prevent a controlled comparison of Agent and VLA paradigms.' 'Public benchmark aggregates do not supply full per-case denominators, inference-call counts, or independent-repeat uncertainty.' 'Gemini’s dexterous sub-suite aggregation remains unresolved.' Agent and VLA/WAM categories are kept on separate leaderboards; the VLA dexterous suite has ten configurations (it is not stated that agents ran the same ten). Scores are reproduced from the public leaderboard, not new runs. Agent harness is Agent2Act (arXiv 2610.27865).

name: ROSWorld
title: ROSWORLD: When Digital Task Competence Meets Physical Execution
org: UTokyo, JD.COM, PKU, SII, FDU, HKU, THU
interface: Each reply is JSON with a short reason and 1–8 actions: robot_step relative Cartesian deltas [dx,dy,dz,rx,ry,rz] (hands add 6 joint targets per hand), wait, done; generic IK + joint drive tracks them on a simulated Franka workstation (rigid probe or dual-arm dexterous hands) that presses a real keyboard/mouse wired to a live OSWorld VM
judged_by: OSWorld official application-state evaluators
trials: 40 tasks × 5 models × 3 conditions (OSWorld, probe, hands), one run each (400 physical episodes); up to 100 model decisions per episode

speed.latency: 'With API-served models, a 100-step physical episode takes 2–5 hours of wall-clock time, most of it model inference.' Physics pauses during model inference.
speed.cost: 400 physical episodes 'occupied 16 RTX 5090 GPUs for about two days'

summary: Couples an Isaac Sim robot workstation to a live OSWorld desktop so the same model does the same 40 tasks by software input and by physically pressing keys and the mouse, under the same official evaluators. 'Models that complete 31-39 tasks on the desktop complete at most 23 with the probe and 28 with the hands': GPT-6 Astra 39 → 23 (probe) / 28 (hands), GPT-6.1 Sol 39 → 15/16, Claude Opus 5.5 39 → 11/3, Kimi K3 and GLM-5.3-Flash 0.
caveats: No separate limitations section. Physics pauses during model inference; one run per model–task–condition; key coordinates, device poses and direct GUI actions are not given to the policy. Authors: 'Misses are the largest failure for every model (27–70% of attempts)' and 'even the strongest models stall on repeated, unverified retries.' Of 304 failed episodes, 239 exhaust the 100-step budget.

name: γ-Scape
title: $γ$-Scape: An Agent-Centric World for Mobile Embodied Intelligence
org: TeleAI (China Telecom), SJTU, CMU, Univ. of Manchester, Gamma Robotics
interface: Agents write programs / tool calls over perception (SAM 3, Contact-GraspNet, Molmo2-8B for CaP-X), navigation, arm/torso/gripper motion tools on a simulated R1 Pro wheeled dual-arm robot; virtual grasp bindings disabled; OWMM-Agent baseline uses its own 8B model
judged_by: BenchForge goal evaluators (final-state and process predicates); semantic progress from evaluator records
trials: 220 instances (22 families × 10); three valid trials per system–task pair, best-of-three reported
summary: Isaac-Sim-based world (370 scenes, 11,073 object assets) with a 22-family, 220-instance mobile-manipulation suite. Three GPT-6-Astra agentic systems and OWMM-Agent are scored: 'RAX achieves the highest overall success (21.8%) and mean semantic progress (39.1%), followed by ASPIRE (15.5% / 34.5%), CaP-X (10.0% / 23.2%), and OWMM-Agent (4.1% / 12.2%).' Also demos contact collection and trace-informed program revision with Codex CLI + GPT-6-Astra.
caveats: No separate limitations section. Best-of-three trials ('selecting one valid trial by success first and semantic progress second'); invalid runs replaced; 'Physics pauses during inference'; system-specific clocks and turn limits; 'These results compare integrated systems, including their tools and budgets.' ASPIRE skill library and RAX exploration artifacts were built on development instances (RAX on same-family packages) and frozen before evaluation. Contact-collection case studies use 'privileged context'. 'Collision checking in RAX’s free-space arm tool is restricted to robot self-collision.'

name: DualManip
title: DualManip: Agentic Dynamic Manipulation via Dual-Path Semantic Reasoning and Geometric Adaptation
org: Tsinghua University, HIT (Shenzhen), Beijing Institute of Control Engineering
interface: VLM decomposes the task into stages, names functional regions (SAM 3 masks) and picks spatial constraints from a predefined relation set; constraint solving + AnyGrasp give poses; a per-object-trained shape-adaptive correspondence network transfers grasp contacts at ~139 ms per update; failed feasibility checks trigger VLM replanning
judged_by: not stated (success counts per task)
trials: 15 trials per object–condition–method; 6 tasks (3 general × static/single-change/continuous, 3 assembly static only); latency averaged over 20 updates

speed.latency: 'DualManip requires 138.7 ms per adaptation'; agentic baseline CLEA 6.376 s with GPT, 4.329 s with local Qwen3.5-2B

summary: KUKA iiwa real-robot study. GPT-5.6 Terra handles infrequent semantic reasoning; a learned geometric path re-targets grasps under motion and deformation, falling back to VLM replanning on failure. Under continuous scene change 'DualManip maintains a 53.3% mean success rate, considerably surpassing ReKep (28.9%) and OmniManip (17.8%), whereas CLEA and Open-loop fail completely'; adaptation is 'approximately 46× faster than agentic verification and semantic replanning'.
caveats: Authors: 'DualManip relies on pre-constructed templates and object-specific training for dense correspondence, constraining direct zero-shot generalization to unseen instances.' Correspondence network trained on 100 RGB-D observations per object per viewpoint. Latency excludes 'shared downstream modules with large runtime variance'. Qwen3.5-2B is used only to time the CLEA baseline.

name: RoboLiveMem
title: RoboLiveMem: Is Robot Memory Solved When the World Does Not Wait?
interface: Realistic tier: tool-using agent (Claude Code or Codex with MCP robot tools; other models in the authors' API agent with the same tools): robot_observe, robot_frames, robot_act(skill, mark), robot_wait, robot_done, with skills acting on numbered marks. Semi-realistic and controlled tiers: one API call per decision issuing scripted skills (pick/place/press; RoboMME skills on a Franka)
judged_by: simulator final-state check (privileged log); a scripted privileged policy validates every seed
trials: 34,176 episodes over 16 models; each instance run once per condition (paused, live, visible-twin live)

speed.latency: median 1.9–4.6 s per decision for the Claude/GPT models on the realistic tier; Gemini 4 Argon and Carbon '32 and 56 s per decision in our own agent'

summary: Runs 29 robot-memory task families (16 BEHAVIOR-1K scenes, a MuJoCo kitchen, ManiSkill/RoboMME tasks) twice: with the simulator paused while the model thinks, as earlier memory benchmarks do, and with the world running. 'when a remembered object changes in a realistic scene, the 8 Claude and GPT models succeed in 97% of episodes on average with the world paused, but in only 50% with the world running', and rankings change: 'Claude Opus 5.5, which never fails when paused, succeeds in 44%'. 'models given only 2 s per decision still fall at least 36 points below their paused success'; most failures are actions on camera frames from before the change ended, and looking again just before acting closes most of the realistic gap.
caveats: Authors: 'All scenes are simulated, other actors follow scripts, the people in the realistic tier have no articulated arms, and latency depends on the load of public model services. Realistic-tier results should be compared within models that run in the same kind of agent.' Claude/GPT run in Claude Code/Codex while other models run in the authors' own agent, so harnesses differ; effort settings differ by model. Skills act on numbered marks, so there is no low-level control. On repeated swaps of identical objects all nine models tested still lose points to memory.
milestone: Paused-simulator results overstated frontier robot memory: with the world running instead of paused, the same 8 Claude and GPT models fell from 97% to 50% success (Claude Opus 5.5: 100% to 44%).

name: ICLWorld
title: ICLWorld: Benchmarking In-Context Learning of Agents from Digital to Physical Worlds
interface: UIverse turns every environment into a user interface: each model runs in its own agent CLI (Claude Code, Codex, etc.) with MCP tools only; for robots it sees head and wrist cameras on a control panel and presses arm buttons (translate/rotate by a step, gripper open/close) in short sequences executed by IK in an Isaac Lab dual-arm simulator; object poses are never given
judged_by: per-task programmatic verifier reading simulator state (hidden from the agent)
trials: 160 tasks (110 computer use, 50 robot) with three rule versions, given as text or video; runs per task not stated
summary: Benchmark of in-context rule learning across computer use and robot use through one harness. 'Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra, succeed on 82% and 76% of computer-use runs but only 27% and 26% of robot-use runs, and a no-rule control reduces success to at most 8%'. GPT-6 Astra 'answers 98% of robot rule questions correctly yet completes only 20% of these tasks'.
caveats: Authors: 'Hand-built environments limit ICLWorld to 160 tasks, ablations use three models, robot tasks run in simulation, and no task yet combines computer and robot use.' The simulation pauses between action batches. Robots are driven through teleoperator-style panel buttons with IK, not skills or code, so robot scores reflect this low-level interface. Each model keeps its own agent CLI, so harnesses differ.

name: WorldLeague
title: WorldLeague: Benchmarking Physical Agency
org: xML Lab, National University of Singapore
interface: VLMs drive a mobile R1 in OmniGibson/BEHAVIOR-1K through WorldHarness (adapted from Show-Harness), choosing parameterized base/arm/trunk/gripper commands executed by position control, IK and assisted grasp; VLAs/WAMs (GR00T-N1.5, π0.5, XR-1, others) use their native controllers
judged_by: evaluator physical predicates on the timestamped trajectory (Interactive Score for partial progress, physical success for full goal)
trials: one episode per system per task at seed 0 (60 tasks for VLMs, 59 for VLA/WAMs); full suite repeated with GPT-6.1-Sol at seed 1

speed.latency: mean 40.80–171.58 min per task for frontier VLMs; world time keeps advancing during inference
speed.cost: API cost per task: Fable 5.2 $26.92, GPT-6-Astra $23.15, GPT-6.1-Sol $5.00

summary: 60 simulated mobile-manipulation tasks scoring 13 VLMs, VLAs and WAMs on the same physical goals, each through its own interface. 'Claude Fable 5.2 achieves 13 of the 60 goals and earns the highest mean Interactive Score (28.58/100)', ahead of GPT-6.1-Sol (22.28) and GPT-6-Astra (20.06); the best learned policy, GR00T-N1.5, scores 8.79. 'Even when VLMs answer every final question correctly, they receive an Interactive Score of zero in 71.8% of those episodes.'
caveats: One episode per system and task; Sol's score 'changes on 11 of 60 tasks' between seeds. VLMs and VLA/WAMs run on different robots and interfaces, so the VLM–VLA gap mixes embodiment and interface with model ('Tying these goals to a single control interface limits which AI systems can be compared'). Every system scores zero on 27 of the 59 common tasks.

name: RUIBench
title: RUIBench: What Makes a Good Robot-Use Interface?
org: Show Lab, National University of Singapore
interface: RUIKit: 13 robot-use interfaces (six action abstractions Joint/Delta/Step/Pose/Point/Skill × per-action replies or Python programs, plus a free-choice RUI), all sharing 24 MCP tools, SAM 3 detection and depth-based localization (no privileged state); Claude Code (Opus 5.5) and Codex (GPT-6 Astra) at high effort; a fine-tuned Qwen3.5-4B as the small-model baseline
judged_by: independent offline scorer on logged trajectories, withheld from the agent (sim); human operator (real)
trials: sim: 30 tasks × 13 RUIs × 5 test missions = 1,950 episodes per frontier agent; real: 650 episodes on a Franka Research 3

speed.latency: sim charges a fixed 8 s per model response; 30 min limit per episode
speed.cost: mean API cost $0.69–$2.37 per episode across RUIs

summary: Controlled study of the interface between a frontier agent and a robot on 30 manipulation tasks. 'changing only the RUI shifts a frontier agent's success rate from 45% to 81%, and that of a fine-tuned 4B model from 13% to 47%', far more than the 2.1-point gap between the two frontier agents averaged across RUIs (Claude Code 70.1%, Codex 72.2%). Interfaces that win in sim do not all transfer to the real robot. Agents often 'declare success despite observable failures'.
caveats: Authors: 'Extending the real-robot study beyond five tasks on one arm would test how widely the observed interface shifts hold'; 'Contact-rich and time-critical tasks remain difficult across nearly all RUIs'; 'Closing the verification gap further requires task-level verifiers'. Only 5 test missions per task-RUI cell in sim; sim latency is a fixed 8 s rather than true model latency; real-robot grader blinding not stated. No VLA baseline.

name: RoboUniverse-10K
title: RoboUniverse-10K: Toward the Scaling Era of Agentic Robotics via Real-to-Sim Environments
org: Tsinghua University; Einsia.AI; Peking University; UIUC; HKU; UCL; UNC-Chapel Hill
interface: Coding agent (GPT models in Codex, others in Claude Code) writes and runs Python in a Harbor-compatible sandbox reaching Isaac Sim only through describe/observe/step/step_chunk/finish; joint-level actions on a Franka or dual-arm AgileX, with images and joint state; ground-truth object states and verifier hidden
judged_by: hidden task-specific verifier on final simulator state; the 500 test tasks manually verified by human experts
trials: RoboUniverse-Verified: 500 held-out tasks (200 single-arm, 300 dual-arm), one attempt per task per model; real: one qualitative Franka demo

speed.latency: simulation paused during model inference
speed.cost: SFT used 'approximately 1,500 equivalent NVIDIA H100 GPU hours'

summary: 10,807 verifiable Isaac Sim environments built by an automated Real2Sim pipeline from real robot videos, with 500 held-out expert-verified tasks as RoboUniverse-Verified. 'GPT-6.2 Astra and Claude Opus 5.5 achieve overall success rates of 85.8% and 76.8%, GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol reach 54.6% and 49.4%'; open baselines reach 2.6% to 10.0%. SFT of Qwen3.6-35B-A3B on ~17K GPT-6 Astra trajectories lifts it 'from 0.8% to 21.2%'.
caveats: Authors: 'the reconstructed simulation scenes remain relatively simplified, and the dynamics of complex objects are not yet faithfully captured', and the collection 'currently focuses on short, atomic manipulation skills'. Simulation time advances only during step calls (paused during inference). GPT models run in Codex and others in Claude Code, so harness and model are confounded. Environments and verifiers are agent-built; test tasks come from the same pipeline as training data. Real-robot evidence is a single qualitative demo.

name: X-Harness
title: Toward Agentic Robotics: A Large-Scale Study of Harness Design for Robot-Use Agents
org: Google; Emory University; USC; University of Florida; University of Chicago; UC Santa Barbara; Ohio State University; UAB
interface: VLM writes closed-loop Python policy code on training episodes, evolved over up to 8 gated rounds and then frozen; code calls perception tools, motion primitives and a frozen VLA/WAM via language sub-goals; at test time the VLM is called never (Offline), on failure triggers (Semi-online) or per sub-goal (Full-online)
judged_by: each benchmark's own success check (sim); real: replay on held-out recordings plus live chunk checks
trials: over 470,000 rollouts across eight simulation benchmarks; at least 20 test episodes per cell

speed.latency: Offline code runs at native control rate (16.7–25 Hz) vs 0.5–10 Hz for in-loop VLM designs
speed.cost: '$95.6K in logged VLM API list-price spend' for the study; evolution needs '350k–440k tokens, and 1.1–1.5 GPU-hours per task'

summary: Seven controlled, one-factor-at-a-time studies of policy-harness design 'across eight simulation benchmarks, six VLMs, and 15 VLA/WAM checkpoints'. Frontier VLMs predict 3D gripper poses poorly, so the composed X-Harness recipe has the VLM write closed-loop code around a frozen VLA/WAM, 'lifting base policies up to +42.8 points across memory, reasoning, and domain shifts' (VLABench π0.5 25.5 → 68.3 with Opus 5.5); LIBERO-PRO pooled 58.6 → 95.4 (Opus 5.5 over π0.5).
caveats: No dedicated limitations section. Training-time failure reports can include simulator diagnostics (ground-truth poses, oracle masks), never at test time and not on RoboDojo. Code is evolved per task on 5–40 training episodes, so this is not zero-shot. Baselines were rerun by the authors and sometimes differ from official leaderboards. Real-robot validation is mostly replay of held-out recordings, with no physical success table.

name: RoboHarness-Zero
title: Body and Soul: Decoupling Robotic Brain and Policy with RoboHarness-Zero
org: Polyadic Research Group; CUHK-Shenzhen; HKUST; NVIDIA; Xiaohongshu
interface: Frozen VLA controls by default; at checkpoints the VLM sees camera views and robot state, judges progress, rewrites the instruction on stalls and, as a fallback, runs short generated code over generic motion primitives before handing back; fixed supervision rules with a thin per-policy adapter and auto-profiled skill configuration
judged_by: RoboCasa365 environment success predicate
trials: Xiaomi-Robotics-1: 200 paired scenes; four other policies: 50-scene shared subset

speed.latency: average 71 VLM requests per episode; 'waiting for responses consumes 87% of episode wall time'

summary: A task-agnostic VLM supervision harness around frozen VLAs. 'On 200 RoboCasa365 scenes, RoboHarness-Zero with GPT-6 Astra raises the success rate of frozen Xiaomi-Robotics-1 from 57.5% to 70.5% and preserves 90.4% of its standalone successes (104/115) while rescuing 37 of 85 failures' (GPT-6.1 Sol: 63.0%; a no-VLM reissue control: 56.5%). On a 50-scene subset the same rules 'add 8 to 10 percentage points to each of four other frozen policies'.
caveats: Authors: 'We developed the harness with Xiaomi, so the higher rescue rate on Xiaomi could reflect either Xiaomi's capabilities or design choices informed by that policy'; transfer evidence is '50 simulated scenes per new policy and one competing harness'; 'Recovery remains a bottleneck'. Development episodes cover 47 of 50 tasks and 10 eval scenes match development scenes. Simulation only.

name: RegHarness
title: RegHarness: Regulating What Code-as-Policy Agents Keep from Steps to Skills
org: Xiamen University Malaysia; Beijing Zhongke Huiling Robot Technology; Institute of Automation, CAS
interface: Two-level harness around the RATs Code-as-Policy agent team: within a trial, each proposed step is tested from a reset scene with committed steps replayed, and a fixed-rule controller commits it only if the verifier and a task-long LLM auditor approve (all run-time roles on deepseek-flash); between runs, Claude Opus 5.5 in Claude Code turns logged failures into default-off revisions of skills, primitives and rules that the authors choose to enable
judged_by: benchmark task check (LIBERO-PRO / MolmoSpaces), also read by the controller during execution; real: operator on site
trials: LIBERO-PRO: 180 paired trials (60 tasks × 3 initial states), 300 over 5 states; MolmoSpaces: 200; real Kinova Gen3: 3 tasks × 15 trials

speed.latency: 'takes 66 minutes on average against 50' per LIBERO-PRO trial (vs RATs)
speed.cost: 'an estimated CNY 2.16 (US$0.32)' per trial in run-time model calls

summary: With 'a single low-cost model across all run-time roles, RegHarness achieves an 87.8% success rate (158/180) on paired LIBERO-PRO trials, compared with 39.4% for RATs, and a 72.0% success rate on MolmoSpaces trials'. A 2×2 ablation 'shows that its skill refinement alone increases RATs' successful trials from 71 to 135, whereas run-time governance alone achieves 105 and RATs' native stepwise reset-and-replay mode achieves only 46'. Real Kinova Gen3: 28 of 45 vs 21 for RATs, 'a difference not significant at this sample size'.
caveats: Authors: 'Reset-and-replay is currently limited to simulation'; both levels were debugged on initial state 0, so 'the observed gain from skill refinement may be an upper estimate'; refinement 'is gated by the authors and lacks the automatic acceptance test'; the coding agent 'reads success checks, full logs and, on MolmoSpaces during design, the benchmark's ground truth'; all systems read the task check during execution. Perception uses simulator camera extrinsics and noise-free depth. All MolmoSpaces trials are in-sample. LIBERO-PRO here is the 60 Object/Goal/Spatial tasks only.

name: RoboEvo²
title: RoboEvo$^2$: Recursive Robot Self-Improvement via Harness-Policy Co-Evolution
org: HKU; Zhejiang University; SUSTech; CUHK-Shenzhen; City University of Hong Kong
interface: GPT-6 Astra (xhigh) repairs failures of a π0.5 policy by writing programs on CaP-X/RATs robot APIs along Code, Code+ICL and Code+Policy routes, consolidated into skills, routing and memory; verified trajectories then fine-tune the policy (with counterfactual preference distillation); in hybrid mode each step is routed to the policy or a code skill
judged_by: task-level success check (simulator) for selecting training data and for evaluation; real-world judge not stated
trials: LIBERO-PRO: 8 settings × 100 episodes on unseen initial states; RoboTwin C2R: 5,000; Unitree G1-D: 4 tasks × 10 trials

speed.cost: per-round coding-agent 'API expenditure decreases from $430.63 to $98.92' on LIBERO-PRO

summary: Co-evolves a code harness and a learned policy without extra human demonstrations: 'RoboEvo2 improves standalone success from 11.0% to 84.1% and hybrid success from 30.4% to 90.5% on LIBERO-PRO, with similar gains and reduced agentic costs on RoboTwin C2R', and reaches '95.0% hybrid success on the Unitree G1-D'. On the G1-D the policy trained on 120 automatically collected demonstrations scores 85.0% standalone vs 80.0% for π0.5 trained on 200 teleoperated ones. Swapping the agent for Qwen3.8-27B gives 76.0% / 82.5% on LIBERO-PRO.
caveats: Authors: skills are built 'on top of a fixed set of atomic skills and perception tools, which do not yet cover capabilities such as force-controlled contact or in-hand regrasping'; 'A task-level success check selects the executions that train the policy'. The agent gets rendered depth and camera calibration. Hybrid numbers still call an agent at test time. Comparisons with other methods 'retain their original evaluation protocols'. Real-world: 10 trials per task, judge not stated. Code 'will be publicly released'.

name: Agent on Guard (AoG)
title: Agent on Guard: Self-Improving Runtime Intervention for Robust Robotic Manipulation
org: USTC; LeapWing AI; MBZUAI; Institute of Automation, CAS
interface: GPT-6 Astra (xhigh) watches a frozen policy (VPP2 WAM on RoboDojo-Sim, Xiaomi-Robotics-1 on RoboCasa365, fine-tuned π0.5 on the real robot) on a shared physical clock, takes over with Python recovery programs and hands back; over 5 self-improvement rounds it revises intervention rules, recovery programs and handover conditions; both models stay frozen
judged_by: benchmark success criteria and Score (RoboDojo-Sim, RoboCasa365); real: full task completion without human intervention (judge not named)
trials: RoboDojo-Sim: 42 tasks × 50 episodes; RoboCasa365: 50 tasks × 50; real AgileX PiPER: 3 tasks × 20 trials

speed.latency: 20.2 min end-to-end per episode vs 103.0 for the GPT-6 Astra agent (dev set)
speed.cost: 1.204M online tokens per episode vs 8.096M for the GPT-6 Astra agent, excluding self-improvement cost

summary: A programming agent decides when to intervene on a frozen robot policy and when to hand back. 'On RoboDojo-Sim, AoG achieves a success rate of 50.57% and a task score of 57.26, exceeding the strongest evaluated baseline by 11.22 percentage points and 10.68 points' (frozen VPP2 alone 32.26%; GPT-6 Astra agent alone 22.48%), and 'reduces end-to-end episode latency by 80.4% and online token consumption by 85.1% relative to the GPT-6 Astra agent'. RoboCasa365: Xiaomi-Robotics-1 57.4% → 69.6%.
caveats: No limitations section; labelled a LeapWing AI technical report. 'The initial harness underperforms the standalone policy' before self-improvement. The harness is evolved per benchmark and policy–agent pair; whether self-improvement episodes are disjoint from test scenes is not stated. The GPT-6 Astra baseline matches Zhang et al.'s published run exactly (likely copied, not stated). The world keeps running while the agent reasons; no privileged simulator state.

name: EvoMisty
title: EvoMisty: Building, Optimizing, and Evolving Capabilities on a Social Robot
interface: Plugin for Claude Code (Opus 5.5) and Codex (GPT-6 Astra): the agent reads Misty II documentation, writes a control program, verifies each capability on the physical robot, writes task programs from the capability and skill libraries, and optimizes them on user-specified metrics
judged_by: agent-written automatic checks plus human checks for anything seen or heard; optimisation metrics measured by the authors on held-out data
trials: 28 AutoMisty tasks + 7 new tasks on one physical Misty II; attempts per task not stated
summary: Coding agents build a social robot's capabilities from its documentation and verify them on hardware. 'The two agents construct 109 and 107 verified atomic capabilities, respectively. Both complete all 28 AutoMisty benchmark tasks and seven additional tasks beyond AutoMisty's capabilities.' 'Optimization improves all seven evaluated metrics across five tasks', e.g. 'dialogue response latency decreases by 52% and 71%'.
caveats: Authors: 'the applicability of EvoMisty to other robot platforms remains to be validated'; 'Capability verification and task completion checks still rely on human observation and feedback'. Tasks are mostly speech, display and base motion, with no manipulation. The AutoMisty baseline was rerun by the authors. Code 'coming soon'.

name: AA-Robotics-Sim
title: Can language models drive a humanoid robot? Introducing AA-Robotics-Sim v0.1
interface: 'Stirrup agent harness with shell and image-viewing tools; the same harness and prompts for every model'. The model writes Python that sends reference poses to a simulated Unitree G1 humanoid; 'NVIDIA GEAR SONIC, which keeps the robot balanced and tracks the reference poses the model sends', handles whole-body control; one head RGB-D camera
judged_by: per-task scoring scripts on simulator physics measurements, 0–100 with partial credit (Artificial Analysis)
trials: 10 tasks; 5 practice episodes then 10 evaluation episodes on new scenes per task

speed.latency: GPT-6.2 Sol 17.3 min per evaluation episode (fastest); Gemini 4 Argon 39 min (slowest)
speed.cost: per evaluation episode: GPT-6.2 Sol $0.98, GPT-6.2 Astra $3.90, Claude Opus 5.5 $4.62, Claude Fable 5.2 $9.01

summary: Independent simulated-humanoid benchmark in which frontier models in a coding-agent harness control a Unitree G1 over a learned whole-body controller across embodied reasoning, pick and place, assembly/tool use and mobility. Overall scores: GPT-6.2 Astra 71.0, Claude Fable 5.2 57.5, GPT-6.2 Sol 53.7.
caveats: 'research preview'; simulation only; 'Practice ran on an earlier version of the environment and is scored with the current scoring rules'; 'there is no LiDAR and no stereo pair'. Pick and place is the weakest group for every model, mainly because secure grasps with the three-fingered hands are hard. No VLA baseline. Effort settings not stated.

name: MARGIN
title: MARGIN: A Risk-Aware Agent for Robot Program Refinement
org: Tsinghua University; Peng Cheng Laboratory; Southern University of Science and Technology; Institute of Automation, CAS
interface: Claude Opus 5.5 coding worker (ASPIRE reproduction) writes robot programs over perception, grasp-synthesis and motion-planning tools; after development success saturates, MARGIN ranks programs by near-miss margin (step budget left in the slowest successful development rollout), asks the worker for repairs, and accepts only revisions that keep development success and raise the margin
judged_by: benchmark success check (LIBERO-Pro / LIBERO-90 / Robosuite) on held-out and fresh seeds; acceptance uses development seeds only
trials: LIBERO-Pro: 80 tasks, held-out seeds 1–50 (4,000 episodes) plus fresh seeds 101–130; repairs on 37 tasks over two rounds (74 sessions); also 90 LIBERO-90 and 7 Robosuite tasks

speed.cost: 'Repairing a program costs $4.4–6.0 per task, compared with $12.5–15.8 for the ASPIRE discovery campaign'; $338 total refinement

summary: Adds risk-aware refinement to agentic robot-program debugging once binary success saturates: the authors' ASPIRE reproduction with Opus 5.5 'succeeds in 3,927/4,000 LIBERO-Pro held-out episodes for a success rate of 98.175%', yet dev-perfect programs still cause 53 of 73 failures. 'The near-miss margin predicts held-out failures with an AUC of 0.774', and margin-guided repair 'reduces executed control steps by 10.7% and 15.0%' on LIBERO-Pro and '18.0–20.0% on LIBERO-90 and Robosuite'; safe racing cuts candidate-evaluation episodes by 53.5% with identical selections.
caveats: No dedicated limitations section. Gains are mostly in execution length: held-out success moves only 'from 94.0% to 94.8% in round 1 and from 97.5% to 97.7% in round 2' on the refined tasks. Simulation only, 1000-step horizon; baseline LIBERO-Pro scores in the comparison table are taken from the cited papers. Builds on the authors' reproduction of ASPIRE (official Opus 5.5 ASPIRE: 98.75%).

name: RoboClock
title: Roboclock: A Unified Benchmark for Time-Aware Robotic Intelligence
interface: VLMs queried in closed loop through a Tool-augmented EEF interface (tools on visual observations and measured robot state, no privileged simulator state), compared with VLAs/WAMs on the same 16-D joint-position action interface; a Latency-Aligned protocol advances environment time during inference
judged_by: simulator task evaluator (physical and temporal clauses); real pilot: operator scores each episode with a step rubric
trials: 60 tasks × 10 seeds per model at easy level (Isaac Sim); real-robot pilot on an xArm 6: 10 episodes per task, 360 in total

speed.latency: real pilot: 'The median model reply takes 5.1 s, from 3.4 s for Qwen3.8 27B to 16.8 s for DeepSeek V4.1 Flash'
speed.cost: API cost per episode (zero latency): Gemini 4 Argon $0.35, Claude Opus 5.5 $0.57, GPT-6 Astra $1.58, GPT-6.1 Sol $0.24

summary: 60 time-constrained manipulation tasks (Temporal Window, Event-Reactive, Throughput) scored with inference paused (TSR) and with latency charged to the clock (LTSR). Zero-shot, 'Gemini 4 Argon achieves 24.5% PSR and 18.2% TSR through Tool-augmented EEF, while GPT-6 Astra reaches 22.8% and 19.0%', but 'with inference latency included, Gemini and GPT-6 Astra fall to 8.2% and 3.0% LTSR, GPT-6.1 Sol and Claude Opus 5.5 to 2.3% and 1.0%'. The fine-tuned π0.5 keeps '8.3% LTSR against 10.3% TSR' and is the best method overall, but fine-tuned policies barely transfer to the 15 held-out tasks.
caveats: Authors: 'Our evaluation uses simulation with simplified processes and some compressed time scales, so transfer to physical robots remains to be validated. LTSR also depends on inference hardware and serving conditions.' VLMs run with low thinking mode; proprietary models are charged their API latency, open-weight models run on eight A100s, and LTSR changes with API serving speed (App. F.1). The real-robot pilot is described by the authors as descriptive only.

name: ReWeave
title: ReWeave: Emergent Physical Task Topologies for Embodied Harness Optimization and Cross-Task Meta-Distillation
org: Zhejiang University; Stanford University; Tsinghua University; AGIBOT Innovation
interface: Inner LLM controller acts as the policy through a harness (context, workflows, control loop) over a frozen π0.5 VLA, SAM3 perception and Cartesian/IK primitives; an outer LLM agent revises the harness offline between episodes, guided by an emergent task topology that re-scores archived trials
judged_by: official benchmark success labels (sim); real: on-site operator using physical endpoint criteria
trials: LIBERO-PRO 80 tasks and RoboDojo 42 tasks: seed 0 for development (up to 10 rounds per task), held-out seeds 1–10; real dual-arm G2: 10 trials per task and harness version

speed.latency: real G2 sorting episodes 504.3 → 402.1 s
speed.cost: offline tokens reported, e.g. 41.72 M for eight-source distillation

summary: Optimizes an LLM-controlled embodied harness without updating policy weights: 'ReWeave improves held-out success from 89.00% to 98.75% on LIBERO-PRO and from 25.50% to 58.25% on RoboDojo' (RoboDojo Score 63.43), and finds retained progress in 89% of 159 failed RoboDojo development trials. On eight unseen LIBERO-PRO tasks the shared harness reaches 51.3% vs 41.3% for direct distillation, 75.0% after continual learning. On the real G2, sorting rises from 20% to 80% and pouring/plugging (frozen VLA) from 40% to 60% and 50% to 70%.
caveats: Authors: 'Topology inference depends on observable traces, and ambiguous contacts can delay edge resolution. Optimization requires physical trials and model calls. Agent reasoning adds execution latency, limiting use in time-sensitive settings; transfer remains uneven across the hardest tasks.' Harness is optimized per task on seed 0 before held-out testing; comparisons are against the authors' own seed harness H0 rather than re-run external systems; archived LIBERO-PRO development records contain simulator state used for post-hoc reference predicates (withheld from scorer and optimizer). Real-robot results are 10 trials per task.

name: Next-Manip
title: Next-Manip: On-Demand Agent-Policy Collaboration for Robotic Manipulation
interface: A lightweight GPT-6 Luna classifier (Agent Invocation Controller) allocates each action chunk to either GPT-6 Astra acting directly or a learned policy (Simate VLA on RoboDojo, EventVLA on RMBench, fine-tuned π0.5 on the real arm); both execute the first ten actions per chunk; compact task references from demonstrations guide both
judged_by: benchmark native success criteria (sim); real: recorded operator labels
trials: RoboDojo: 12 representative tasks × 20 trials; RMBench: 9 tasks × 20 trials; real xArm7: 4 tasks × 20 trials

speed.cost: 28.80 Astra calls per episode on RoboDojo, '62.5% fewer than the 76.72' with Astra alone; Luna classifier input cost below 1% of Astra's

summary: Decouples when to call the frontier agent from the agent itself. On 12 RoboDojo tasks 'Next-Manip achieves 59.58% success and a Score of 67.88', above published standalone Astra (14.83%) and Simate (38.56%) and leaderboard leader Q0-Preview (53.50%); RMBench 94.4% vs 67.9% for EventVLA and 64.4% for local Astra. Real world: 'raising the average success rate from 28.75% to 77.50%' over policy-only π0.5.
caveats: Authors: 'Next-Manip adopts frozen models as executors, and its performance is therefore constrained by their capabilities.' RoboDojo uses a 12-task subset chosen by Astra leaderboard strata; locally reproduced baselines and ablations use 5 trials per task while Next-Manip uses 20; leaderboard baselines were not re-run. Real-world policy is fine-tuned per task on 50 demonstrations.

name: Atomic Policy
title: Atomic Policy: Composing Atomic Manipulation Skills with Agentic Reasoning
interface: A VLM estimates symbolic state and goal, a PDDL solver builds a skill plan, and an agentic harness steers each learned phase skill (diffusion policy, MolmoBot or π0.5) with language and MolmoPoint visual points; a separate VLM checker verifies each phase and triggers replanning
judged_by: benchmark success checks (sim); real: task score from completed grasp/place steps (scorer not stated)
trials: sim: 50 seeded episodes (direct-control comparison), 200 rollouts per configuration on MolmoSpaces; real Franka Panda: 3 tasks × 20 trials (10 ID, 10 OOD) per method

speed.latency: real: checker queried every 128 control steps; authors note VLM and pointing inference 'adds latency'

summary: Composes learned atomic skills under VLM planning and checking. Replanning matters on dependent phases: on simulated Tabletop success 'falls from 64.0% to 17.8% without replanning'. On real OOD Crossword 'both end-to-end baselines obtain zero task score, while Atomic + MolmoBot and Atomic + π0.5 reach 72.5 and 60.0'. In a controlled comparison with zero-shot gpt-6-astra emitting end-effector displacements, 'Direct control reaches 98.0% success on Push 5 Blocks, compared with 86.3% for Atomic Policy, whereas Atomic Policy reaches 60.0% success ... on Tabletop, compared with 52.0%'.
caveats: Authors: 'The phase set, PDDL domain, and checker prompts are specified manually for each task family, and demonstrations require phase and point annotations. Execution depends on the accuracy of the VLM and pointing model, whose inference also adds latency.' Real-robot results are 10 trials per task and condition. Planner/checker VLM differs by task (gemini-3.8-flash on Push 5 Blocks and MolmoSpaces, gpt-6-astra on Tabletop and real robot).

name: Boundary-Aware Policy Learning
title: Boundary-Aware Policy Learning for Agent-Orchestrated Robot Manipulation
org: University of Electronic Science and Technology of China; Shanghai AI Laboratory; Tongji University; Shanghai Innovation Institute
interface: Claude Opus 5.5 (high effort) acts only through registered tools (images, SAM 3 segmentation, pixel-to-world, motion-planner end-effector moves, gripper) and hands over to a π0.5 policy trained only on contact segments from diverse start poses, following a short handoff protocol that describes the policy's boundary; the policy is later retrained on curated successful system rollouts
judged_by: benchmark success checks (RoboTwin 2.0, RoboDojo official implementation); real: single qualitative episode
trials: RoboTwin 2.0: 50 tasks × 10 episodes per setting; RoboDojo: 26 Gen/Mem/Open tasks × 10 episodes

speed.latency: agent-direct trials take a median 18.2 min (RoboTwin 2.0) and 32.8 min (RoboDojo), with LLM inference 93.0% and 86.5% of total time; self-improvement cuts time per episode by 37.5% on average
speed.cost: $1.53 per episode for Claude Opus 5.5 (high) on the 30-task subset; self-improvement cuts API cost by 41.3%; collecting the self-improvement data cost about $1,013

summary: Makes the policy's handoff boundary wide and explicit so the agent hands over only contact segments. Versus Harness VLA, the system is '26.4 percentage points higher on RoboTwin 2.0 under the official randomized configuration (C2R)' (98.4% vs 72.0%) and '28.4 percentage points higher on average on RoboDojo' (69.2% vs 40.8%). Swapping the agent with the policy fixed: 'the four other language models reach 67.7% to 85.0% without retraining the policy, compared with 98.7% for Claude Opus 5.5'.
caveats: Authors: data curation discards suboptimal rollout segments, and 'the handoff protocol describes the boundary only by rules'. Real-robot deployment is a single qualitative episode ('we leave a quantitative evaluation on real robots to future work'). RoboDojo results exclude the long-horizon and precision subsets; RoboDojo needed a hand-written scripted expert to collect contact-segment data. Tasks are explored before evaluation and notes merged into a frozen memory.

name: SkillHarness
title: SkillHarness: Execution-Aware Coordination with Plug-and-Play Skills for Long-Horizon Traversal
org: Fudan University; Lenovo Group Limited; Nanyang Technological University; Shanghai Jiao Tong University
interface: Event-triggered harness: a local Gemma 4 E2B monitor triggers asynchronous DeepSeek V4.1 Flash planning, which proposes navigation and locomotion-skill switches; proposals pass geometric feasibility and execution-phase admission checks before a library of perceptive-RL locomotion skills executes them
judged_by: route success criteria (clear all obstacles in order, permitted contacts only, stop within tolerance before deadline); scorer not stated
trials: physical robot: 8 route conditions × 10 trials; ablation N=2–5 terrain types × 10 trials per setting; Isaac Sim ablation: 50 trials per setting

speed.latency: Gemma monitor median 1.289 s per classification
speed.cost: estimated US$0.00234 per planning request (10,000 input / 100 output tokens) vs US$0.021 for GPT-6.1 Sol

summary: An LLM-guided harness picks and admits learned locomotion skills for multi-terrain traversal. In Isaac Sim the harness check gives '90% (45/50), compared with 24% (12/50) without Harness'; on the physical robot with refined rules 'the robot completed all ten trials at every N', versus 5/10, 1/10, 0/10 and 0/10 without the harness. SkillHarness completed all ten trials in each of eight route conditions where MGDP and REAL fell to 20–60% at K=5.
caveats: No dedicated limitations section. The MGDP and REAL baselines run in MX simulation while SkillHarness runs on the physical robot, and the authors note the structured and unstructured routes were not matched in difficulty. Harness rules were refined from the five failed simulation trials before the physical tests. Robot platform is not named in the text.

name: JiL (Judgment-in-the-Loop)
title: Calibrating World Action Models: From Adaptive System 2 Takeover to Self-Evolution
org: Central South University; ACE Robotics; University of Sydney; UC San Diego
interface: A judgment token on a frozen world action model (Fast-WAM, LingBot-VA, Kairos) predicts chunk success; below threshold, a GPT-6-Astra-based RGB-D agent takes over and executes modular actions (grasp, re-grasp, place, sweep) from the live state, handing back when confidence recovers; successful takeovers are distilled into a repair WAM that runs with zero agent calls
judged_by: benchmark success checks (RoboTwin 2.0, LIBERO-Plus); real-world scorer not stated
trials: RoboTwin 2.0 full (50 tasks, Clean and Random) and LIBERO-Plus full; real AgileX Piper: 3 tasks × 50 trials per method

speed.latency: judgment token 1.6 ms per chunk; mean episode time 31.4 s (JiL System 1 & 2) vs 94.6 s for full GPT-6 Astra and 16.8 s for the base WAM (RoboTwin 2.0, Fast-WAM)

summary: Calls the frontier agent only when the WAM's calibrated confidence drops. At a 30% agent-call budget on RoboTwin 2.0 JiL lifts Fast-WAM from 39.8% to 74.5% ('cutting Fast-WAM failures on RoboTwin 2.0 by 57.6% ... vs. 16.3% for random calls'), against 88.4% for the GPT-6 Astra agent in full control; on Kairos it reaches 89.8%, 'surpassing even the 100% pure GPT-6-Astra agent'. Distilled standalone WAMs gain '+13.1% to +24.7% with zero agent calls'. Real world: JiL System 1 & 2 82.0% and 86.0% vs base WAM 44.0% and 50.7% and full Astra 89.3%.
caveats: No dedicated limitations section. All two-system baselines share the same base WAM, agent and 30% chunk-level budget, but the GPT-6 Astra agent's tool stack is described only briefly (RGB-D 3D pose estimation plus modular manipulation actions). Real-world evaluation uses three tasks on one arm; who scored success is not stated.

name: Weight-Space Programming for RFMs
title: Sparks of Weight-Space Programming for Robot Foundation Models
interface: Claude Opus 5.5 with tool access runs the π0.5 policy server in RoboTwin 2.0, inspects actions and action-expert neuron activations, and directly rewrites connections to near-silent neurons so a corrective movement fires in the diagnosed failure state; no demonstrations, fine-tuning or gradient updates; the edited π0.5 is the policy
judged_by: simulator success on new seeded scenes against a pass mark set in advance; failures identified from the simulator's exact measurements
trials: held-out scenes: 200 (beat_block_hammer), 300 (click_bell), 200 (move_can_pot), 505 (place_mixed_objects_basket); paired with the unedited policy, plus random and sign-reversed controls
summary: An LLM agent repairs recurring π0.5 failures by editing about 6,000 of 3.35 billion parameters. 'Three of the five fixes clearly worked on unseen scenes': hammer 56.5% → 70.5% (200 scenes), bell 87.3% → 96.7% (300 scenes), and on an already task-fine-tuned basket checkpoint 67.7% → 84.4% across 505 scenes. Sign-reversed edits recreated the targeted failure and random edits 'made no consistent difference'.
caveats: Authors: the approach 'worked best when the failure situation was recognizable and a simple correction could address it; it did not solve every failure' (move_can_pot 38% → 41%, not significant; turn_switch never reached held-out testing). Edits are task-specific and diagnosed using the simulator's exact measurements; simulation only. Short report (8 pages); the PDF's own title differs from the arXiv title.

name: Mibot-RUA
title: Mibot-RUA (Mibot_RSI): RoboDojo agent-track entry
interface: Eval-only XPolicyLab adapter: 'an agent entry: GPT-6-Astra through the Responses API' runs its session in a subprocess and moves the arx_x5 robot through TASK_ENV.take_action with joint targets; it mounts knowledge snapshots built by practicing on seed-0 layouts plus a priors.json of 27 short scene notes
judged_by: RoboDojo simulator checker (official leaderboard)
trials: RoboDojo sim, 42 tasks; adapter PR's own run: seed 1, 42 tasks × 50 episodes (2,100 episodes)
summary: Robot-use agent from Xiaomi Robotics built on GPT-6 Astra, added to the RoboDojo sim leaderboard's agent track on 2026-11-26 at 'Avg. (w/o Open): 83.94 / 79.33%' (score / success rate), the top agent-track entry. The adapter PR's own seed-1 run reports SR 78.43% / Score 83.75 including Open tasks.
caveats: Starred by RoboDojo as deviating from the agent-track rules: the runtime injects '34 task-specific distilled briefs ... 289 task-specific skills ... 7,231 task-specific dev experience entries, 65 task-specific vision/geometry tools' and 'Task-specific scene and mechanism priors beyond Detail Description', including opponent move triggers and simulator-step behaviour. Testing began before the 2026-11-14 agent-track rules took effect. Open tasks are not in the leaderboard average. PR: 'Model outputs are non-deterministic'. No paper or company write-up; PR #204 is still open.

name: RoboSpoof
title: You Can't See Everything: Perceptual Attacks on Embodied AI
org: Robocurve; University of Southern California; UC Irvine
authors: Christopher Leet, Joshua Holder, Achyutha Menon, Anton de la Fuente, Sven Koenig, Tzu Kit Chan, Jay Chooi
interface: Inspect Robots: move_to (Cartesian end-effector), done and give_up tools on a bimanual I2RT YAM; proprioception plus three 224 × 224 px cameras; 15-action budget
judged_by: Claude Fable 5.1 classified each trial as attempt or refusal
trials: 5 unsafe tasks (from RoboHarm) × 12 trials × 3 footage conditions per model; 900 trials
summary: Tests whether frontier models driving a real robot in closed loop refuse unsafe tasks when camera footage is blurred or doctored. Models attempted unsafe tasks in 81/300 trials (27%) on unaltered footage, 263/300 (88%) with a Gaussian blur and 291/300 (97%) with frame-by-frame doctoring: 'models rarely refuse tasks unless visual observations provide positive evidence that the tasks are unsafe.'
caveats: Refusal is judged by an LLM (Claude Fable 5.1); 12 trials per cell on one bench; an attempt counts as completed when the model calls done and 'we did not check the scene afterwards'. No date on the paper or page; per-model numbers only in a figure.

name: SOLVE
interface: Training-free multimodal LLM agent writes a sparse, ordered sequence of 6-DoF end-effector keyposes per call, observes the result and writes the next; a motion planner interpolates; keyposes grounded by sparse depth queries (triangulation, stereo or monocular depth); reflects on rollouts and distils a few rules per task
judged_by: RoboDojo / RoboLab simulator checkers; real-robot judge not stated
trials: RoboDojo official run: seed 3, 2,100 episodes (50 per task); RoboLab: 120 tasks × 5 episodes; real UR12e: 16 tasks, 85 episodes

speed.latency: 'each model call takes seconds'; real robot averages 21.9 calls and 6.6 minutes per episode
speed.cost: $1.7 per episode with GPT-6 Astra, $0.5 with GPT-6.1 Sol (list prices), vs $21.1 cited for GPT-6 Astra Direct

summary: 'SOLVE reaches state-of-the-art performance of 74.5% on RoboDojo and 84.5% on RoboLab, with only $1.7 per episode on average, 12x less than previous dense-control agent policies.' On a real UR12e 'the same agent achieves an 88% success rate (75 of 85 episodes) over 16 challenging zero-shot tasks.' Ablation on RoboDojo: the RoboProbe GPT-6 Astra baseline at 22.9% (154.6 calls) rises to 49.5% with sparse keyposes alone and 68.3% with query points and notes.
caveats: Authors: 'Some real tasks require force or continuous feedback that keyposes cannot provide, and each model call takes seconds.' GPT-6.1 Sol RoboDojo rows are two runs at 5 episodes per task. RoboDojo stars the SOLVE leaderboard entry for injecting task-specific information beyond the official Detail Description (see the robodojo entry). Shirt folding was the weakest real task (6 of 10).
title: SOLVE: Sparse, Ordered Keyposes Make LLM Agents Versatile and Efficient Robot Manipulator

name: SEEK
org: Nanyang Technological University, Microsoft Research, National University of Singapore
interface: Frozen model writes a Self-Evolving Programmatic Policy (executable procedures that pick each action from current observations) and records measured action effects, including failures, in a Persistent Action-Effect Bank; retained procedures act without a model request and are revised from the evidence when they meet uncovered conditions
judged_by: RoboDojo task score and strict SR; real robot: operator scores each episode with predefined rules
trials: RoboDojo 42 tasks: 10 evolution attempts, then 50 evaluation episodes per task; GPT-6.2 Astra: 34 tasks, 5 attempts, 10 episodes per task; real Franka: 4 tasks, 5 attempts, 10 unseen episodes per task

speed.latency: GPT-6.2 Astra: 14.1 model requests per episode vs 63.2 acting directly

summary: On all 42 RoboDojo tasks, 10 attempts of retained knowledge raise GPT-6 Astra's average score from 27.0 to 54.4 and SR from 19.7% to 48.0%, with gains on 37 of 42 tasks. With GPT-6.2 Astra on 34 tasks, SEEK after 5 attempts reaches score 80.1 / SR 75.0% vs 49.6 / 40.7% acting directly, with 77.6% fewer requests; on a real Franka the average score rises from 66.9 to 83.3.
caveats: Authors: perception tools, executor and action interface are fixed, so results depend on them (e.g. SAM3); only dual-arm simulation and a single-arm Franka were tested; knowledge accumulates per task, and cross-task transfer is not studied. The Claude Opus 5.5 run covers only 3 analysis tasks.
title: SEEK: Self-Evolution through Execution Knowledge for Agentic Robot Manipulation

name: Skeptic
org: University of Amsterdam, South China Normal University
interface: Training-free protocol for code-as-policy skill discovery (programs over SAM 3, Contact-GraspNet and cuRobo APIs): a grounded event log of measured action effects guides repair, and verified promotion requires development success before a skill enters the shared library
judged_by: simulator task-completion predicate; skill admission also checks an independent verifier agent
trials: LIBERO-Pro: 80 tasks, two campaigns per protocol, 50 held-out seeds per task; Robosuite: 7 tasks, 100 evaluation seeds each
summary: Studies a frozen Qwen3.8-27B that falsely declares tasks physically impossible during skill discovery. 'Across 60 audited tasks, the mean number of tasks with false impossibility judgments decreases from 19.5 to 8.5 per campaign. On 80 LIBERO-Pro tasks and seven Robosuite tasks, Skeptic improves held-out success by 14.9 and 11.7 percentage points' (LIBERO-Pro 63.4% with ASPIRE to 78.3%).
caveats: Authors: only one model and two simulated benchmarks; five other open-weight models of similar size did not complete the original discovery loop; whether gains 'carry over to other compact models and to real robots remains to be tested'; a gap to frontier proprietary models remains.
title: Skeptic: Grounding Failure Diagnosis for Robot Skill Discovery

name: AWAIT
org: University of Science and Technology of China
interface: Black-box VLM agents (native tool-calling agent picking arm/gripper targets from RGB-D, CaP-X, PyRUA-Lean, Q0-Preview) on two AgileX PiPER arms in Isaac Sim; decision and execution time count against the task's action window
judged_by: host-side task judges, isolated from the methods
trials: 18 tasks × 6 scene instances; 648 measured-time and 1,080 controlled-delay rollouts per method–VLM configuration; human reference by five teleoperators
summary: 18 time-sensitive tasks where success must land inside an action window. At real time (ρ=1) every method–VLM configuration scores 0.0 Overall, against 85.4 for human teleoperation; with time slowed 100×, the best is PyRUA-Lean / GPT-6 Astra at 50.8 (native GPT-6.1 Sol agent 46.1, Q0-Preview / Claude Opus 5.5 43.6, CaP-X / Gemini 3.1 Pro 4.3).
caveats: Authors: zero scores at ρ=1 can hide partial progress; human results use five operators and three instances per task; up to 3% of rollouts were aborted by remote-API timeouts. No learned-policy baselines are evaluated.
title: Action Windows Are Inherently Temporal: A Benchmark for Time-Sensitive Robotic Manipulation

name: RoboInF
org: Tongji University, Shanghai Jiao Tong University
interface: Inference-only agents select semantic skills, image targets and skill parameters through one decision interface; a fixed RGB-D geometric skill executor carries out the motion. Compared with π0.5 and OpenWAM trained on RoboInF-4K
judged_by: task-specific simulator checkers on terminal state, trajectories, contacts and event sequences
trials: 861 test episodes per model (RoboTwin, 8 tasks, 6–12 instruction branches each)
summary: Measures whether policies change behaviour when the instruction changes, scoring task success (TR) and joint success with instruction fidelity (JR). On test_clear GPT-6 Astra averages 17.6 JR / 28.9 TR and Qwen3.8-Flash 8.2 / 14.7; 'All four models exhibit a gap between task completion and faithful execution.'
caveats: Authors: RoboInF-4K 'is limited to 4,242 demonstrations across eight tasks'. Agents use a fixed skill executor rather than acting directly; π0.5 and OpenWAM are post-trained on the benchmark's own data, so the comparison is not like-for-like.
title: RoboInF: A Benchmark for Instruction Fidelity in Robotic Manipulation

name: DeCoNav-Act
org: TeleAI, Tongji University, Fudan University, Shanghai Jiao Tong University, Zhejiang University, University of Manchester
interface: Program-as-policy agents (ASPIRE-SG, RAX-SG, the authors' CoMoMa) compose registered navigation and manipulation tools for each robot and revise from execution feedback, coordinating through a team board or shared task graph
judged_by: automated evaluator auditing final-state goal predicates and the execution trace, not the controller's completion flags
trials: 100 test tasks, one episode per task per method; diagnostics 98 trials per method and condition; 20 min model time and 500 s sim time per episode
summary: 500 multi-robot mobile-manipulation tasks in Isaac Sim (Galaxea R1 Pro, TidyBot, Create 3). 'With GPT-5.6-luna no method completes a task, at most 8.8% of dependencies are reached, and even from pre-handoff states no handoff is completed; with GPT-6.1-sol, CoMoMa establishes the condition in 26.5% of trials, but only 4.1% succeed.'
caveats: Authors: test tasks were chosen to be comparatively easy; the handoff diagnostic starts from pre-handoff states; the Oracle-guided setting gives privileged object poses, grasp states and waypoints. CoMoMa is the authors' own method.
title: DeCoNav-Act: Benchmarking Collective Physical Capability in Multi-Robot Mobile Manipulation

name: RESET
interface: From one real demonstration, rebuild a MuJoCo world and a frozen read-only success criterion, check it by open-loop replay, then Claude Code evolves white-box task graphs and skill code from per-node failure evidence; frozen code is deployed with zero runtime LLM calls
judged_by: read-only scorer derived from the demonstrated final state (criterion confirmed once per task by a person); real-robot judge not stated
trials: sim: 8 tasks × 50 unseen layouts; real: 10 trials per task, 280 trials on 4 robots

speed.latency: zero runtime LLM calls

summary: 'On 8 manipulation tasks, each rebuilt from one real demonstration, RESET achieves 97% average success on unseen layouts in simulation, whereas zero-shot code reaches 27%, per-task fine-tuned pi0.5 policies 31%, and Diffusion Policy 50%.' On real robots 223 of 280 trials succeed (80%; fixed-base 210 of 240), with Unitree G1 lowest at 13/40.
caveats: Authors: targets 'rigid, articulated, and quasi-static sweeping tasks, not deformable cloth or dynamic throwing'; contact-topology changes are beyond parameter randomization; practice does not model the humanoid's whole-body controller; Examine is a check, not a guarantee, and missed three enlarged worlds.
title: RESET: One Demonstration, One Verified World, Self-Improved Skills Across Embodiments

name: Paper context for LLM quadruped navigation
interface: Claude Opus 5 writes navigation controllers (behavior trees, edited navigators, controllers from scratch) that command Isaac Sim's frozen Go2FlatTerrainPolicy, with or without research-paper context
judged_by: simulator (trip completion in maze worlds)
trials: setting 3: 8 generations per arm; 1 physics episode per controller, 3 kinematic repetitions
summary: When a maze's shortest route is blocked mid-episode, '2 of 8 controllers written with the context of an incremental-replanning paper complete all four trips under Isaac Sim physics, against 7 of 8 without it (two-sided Fisher's exact test, p = 0.041)'; in a kinematic simulator the two arms are indistinguishable (6/8 vs 5/8).
caveats: Authors call it exploratory: physics results are one episode per controller, kinematic and physics simulators disagreed on 6 of 16 controllers, outputs are non-deterministic, and the environment may be too simple for the paper's efficiency benefit to appear.
title: Does Research-Paper Context Improve LLM-Generated Quadruped Navigation? An Exploratory Simulation Study

name: RoboDojo-Mirror
interface: GPT-6 Astra (medium effort) as a closed-loop tool agent calling move_eef / give_up, cuRobo plans joints, at most 100 decision calls; compared with WALL-OSS, VPP2, Awomo-0.5 and Rex-M1 Preview
judged_by: native RoboDojo task evaluator; real-robot judge not stated
trials: 8 RoboDojo tasks; learned policies 5 layouts × 3 seeds per cell, Astra 5 layouts × 1 rollout per cell; real Franka 10 trials per task and condition (π0.5, FastWAM only)
summary: Adding mirrors to RoboDojo scenes 'reduces aggregate success rates: averaged over the three conditions, the drop ranges from 10.8 to 56.7 percentage points across policies'. The agentic GPT-6 Astra drops least (65.0% to 62.5 / 52.5 / 47.5%), while VLAs/WAMs fall from 60.8–72.5% to as low as 4.2%.
caveats: Authors: execution budgets differ across policies, so aggregates 'should not be interpreted as a controlled cross-policy ranking'; Astra diagnostics use small samples (n=5 or 15); panel controls were run only for WALL-OSS and Awomo-0.5. No frontier model was run on the real robot.
title: Embodied AI Fails the Mirror Test: How a Simple Mirror Breaks Robot Policies

name: RoboARC
org: Northwestern University, Microsoft, UC Berkeley, CMU
interface: Coding agents get only the task instruction, write their own code and send joint or end-effector action chunks through a fixed API; Privileged regime has simulator state and resets, Standard regime has RGB-D and proprioception with one attempt and no resets
judged_by: physics-based automatic grader with verified reference solutions
trials: 90 MuJoCo tasks × 3 domain-randomization seeds, one run per seed; VLAs 216 episodes on 18 one-arm puzzles; real: one buzz-wire task, 8 trials per agent
summary: 90 spatial-constraint puzzles on three robots. 'The strongest agent solved 86% of tasks in the Privileged regime and 43% in the Standard regime' (GPT-6 Astra 85.6 / 42.6; Claude Opus 5.5 80.7 / 29.3), while four zero-shot VLAs (π0.5, MolmoAct2, GR00T N1.7, Cosmos3-Nano-Policy) solve none of their 18 one-arm puzzles.
caveats: Authors: simulation only, with assisted grasps of rigid parts and cloth; one reference solution per task; the real-robot check covers one task. VLAs were run zero-shot after DROID fine-tuning, not trained on the tasks.
title: RoboARC: Physical Puzzles for Robotic Manipulation under Spatial Constraints

name: MFM-VLA
org: University of Science and Technology of China
interface: GPT-6 Astra, queried sparsely, provides target grounding, two-view 3D estimates and grasp verification; analytic controllers execute free-space motion; a fine-tuned VLA (π0.5 / π0) keeps fine-grained manipulation; a calibrated router chooses direct VLA or MFM-assisted execution
judged_by: benchmark environments in sim; real-world judge not stated
trials: LIBERO-PRO 8,000 episodes (50 inits per task); ALOHA-Sim-PRO 50 episodes per condition; RoboCasa365 2,500 episodes; real: 11 glassware tasks × 20 trials per setting
summary: 'Across LIBERO-PRO, ALOHA-Sim-PRO, RoboCasa365, and real-world chemistry tasks, MFM-VLA improves success rates by 14.9, 74.0, 3.6, and 30.9 percentage points, respectively, over the corresponding base VLA' (LIBERO-PRO π0.5 54.9% to 69.8%). Zero-shot GPT-6 Astra control reaches only 3.5% on matched LIBERO-PRO episodes.
caveats: Router needs calibration data; RoboCasa365 Composite-Unseen stays at 2.4%; requires calibrated RGB cameras; relies on a proprietary MFM (GroundingDINO in its place drops assisted success from 73.6% to 16.4%). The VLA is fine-tuned with dense geometric captions and recovery data.
title: Ground, Guide, Act: Improving VLA Spatial Generalization with Multimodal Foundation Models

name: ROAM-Bench
org: HKU, UESTC, Shanghai Innovation Institute, JD.com
interface: VLM chooses predefined navigation and interaction skills (move, strafe, turn, look, open, close, pick, place) or image points; Isaac Sim executes them under motion and collision constraints and returns a new view
judged_by: automatic checks on simulation state and episode records (human audit agreement 97.4% / 93.3%)
trials: 250 tasks per model, single run; human reference on 100 sampled tasks
summary: 250 exploration, counting, geometry and relocation tasks in 27 indoor scenes, scoring outcome and evidence separately. GPT-6 Astra has the highest strict task success at 69.2% (Claude Opus 5.5 40.0%, GPT-6.1 Sol 46.8%), against 84% for humans on a 100-task sample; 29 tasks get no correct answer from any model.
caveats: Single run per model; skills are executed by the simulator, so low-level control is not tested; most task types are spatial question answering rather than manipulation; the human sample is one person per task.
title: ROAM-Bench: Evaluating Embodied Active Spatial Intelligence through Evidence Verification

name: SuperNav-1.5
title: SuperNav-1.5: Structured Spatial Memory For Agentic Navigation Systems
org: Zhejiang University · BYD New Technology Research Institute · Shenzhen University
interface: Frontier MLLM agent makes tool calls to create, update, search and inspect map-grounded memory nodes on an agent-built area-segmented occupancy map, and picks a map marker or memory node as the destination; a geometric executor plans with A* and runs primitive actions; the agent ends each episode with an explicit Stop
judged_by: benchmark metrics in simulator (SR/SPL, 1 m threshold); real robot qualitative only
trials: HM3D-OVON val-unseen 120 episodes; Habitat-GS 150 single- and 150 multi-object episodes; Demand-Bench 200 episodes; each episode run once; ablations on 40 tasks; real Unitree Go2: qualitative demonstrations, no trial counts
summary: Object-goal navigation, not manipulation: a frontier MLLM (GPT-5.6-terra) builds and reuses its own structured spatial memory and hands routes to a geometric executor. On Habitat-GS multi-object episodes it reaches 52.00 SR / 0.2494 SPL vs 34.00 / 0.1388 for SuperNav and at most 4.00 SR for learned navigators (OmniNav, NaVid, Uni-NaVid, StreamVLN); on HM3D-OVON val-unseen 80.00 SR vs 73.33 for SuperNav (3600 s group). Swapping in KIMI-k3-256k or GLM-5.3-flash gives 85.00 and 82.50 SR vs 82.50 on a 40-task ablation.
caveats: Navigation only. Authors: the occupancy map and geometric navigation depend on accurate LiDAR or depth and odometry; sensor errors or drift may distort the geometry. Real-robot results on a Unitree Go2 are demonstrations with no reported trial counts or success rates. Latency and cost not reported. Infrastructure failures are retried.
